name: Dashain
when: Sep–Oct, 15 days ending on the full moon of Ashwin
summary: Nepal's biggest Hindu festival, 15 days in September or October honouring the goddess Durga. Families gather, elders give red tika and jamara barley shoots, kites fill the sky and Kathmandu empties as people head home. For visitors it means clear autumn weather, busy roads and some closed offices.
body: Dashain begins with Ghatasthapana, when families sow barley seeds in a sand-filled pot that sprouts into the yellow jamara used later in the festival. On Phulpati, the seventh day, a procession carries sacred flowers and leaves from Gorkha into Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu Durbar Square. The eighth and ninth days, Maha Asthami and Maha Navami, are the heaviest days of worship at Durga temples, and animal sacrifice still takes place at many shrines, including Taleju and Dakshinkali, which some visitors find hard to watch.

The tenth day, Vijaya Dashami, is the heart of it. Elders place tika, a paste of rice, yoghurt and red vermilion, on the foreheads of younger relatives along with jamara behind the ear, and give blessings and small gifts of money. Families travel across the valley for days to receive tika from every senior relative, and the celebrations continue until the full moon of Kojagrata Purnima. Bamboo swings called linge ping go up in villages, and children fly kites from every rooftop.

For travellers, Dashain falls in the best weather of the year, with clean air after the monsoon and sharp mountain views from Nagarkot and Chandragiri. The catch is logistics: long-distance buses and domestic flights sell out, Kathmandu's shops and some restaurants close for three to five days around Dashami, and hotel prices in Pokhara and Nagarkot rise. We plan Dashain trips well ahead and keep drives short on the main tika days.
tips: Book flights and hotels at least eight weeks ahead if your trip overlaps Vijaya Dashami.
Expect many shops, museums and offices in Kathmandu to close for three to five days around the tenth day.
If animal sacrifice troubles you, skip Dakshinkali and Durga temples on Asthami and Navami mornings.

faqs.q: When is Dashain in 2026?
faqs.a: Dashain follows the lunar calendar and usually falls in late September or October. In 2026 Ghatasthapana is expected in mid-October with Vijaya Dashami about ten days later, but exact dates are set by Nepal's calendar committee each year, so check current status before you travel. We confirm the dates when we build your itinerary and plan drives around the main tika days.

faqs.q: Is Dashain a good time to visit Nepal?
faqs.a: Weather-wise it is one of the best times, with clear post-monsoon skies and good mountain views. The drawbacks are crowded transport, higher hotel rates and closures in Kathmandu around the tenth day. If you book early and accept that some shops shut, you get festive streets, kites, swings and the chance to see a Nepali family festival up close.

faqs.q: Can tourists take part in Dashain tika?
faqs.a: Usually only if a Nepali family invites you, since tika is given by elders to relatives. Many guides and hotel staff are happy to explain the ritual, and some homestays include guests. Watching families on their way to temples and relatives' homes on Vijaya Dashami, dressed in new clothes with red tika and jamara, is open to everyone.

faqs.q: Are shops and sights open during Dashain?
faqs.a: Major heritage sites such as Pashupatinath, Boudhanath, Swayambhunath and the Durbar Squares stay open, though they can be crowded with worshippers. Many shops, government offices, banks and some restaurants close for several days around Vijaya Dashami. Hotels and tourist restaurants in Thamel generally keep running. Withdraw cash before the holiday as ATMs sometimes run dry.

name: Tihar
when: Oct–Nov, five days around the new moon of Kartik
summary: The five-day festival of lights in October or November, Nepal's version of Diwali. Crows, dogs and cows are honoured on successive days, houses glow with oil lamps and marigold garlands on Laxmi Puja night, and the festival ends with Bhai Tika between brothers and sisters.
body: Tihar arrives about three weeks after Dashain and has a gentler, brighter feel. The first day, Kag Tihar, honours crows with food left on rooftops. The second, Kukur Tihar, is the day visitors remember: dogs across Kathmandu, pets and strays alike, are given marigold garlands, a red tika and a good meal in thanks for their loyalty. The third morning is Gai Tihar, when cows are worshipped, and that evening is Laxmi Puja, when households clean, paint rangoli patterns at the door and light rows of oil lamps to welcome the goddess of wealth.

On Laxmi Puja night and the nights that follow, groups of children and young people go house to house singing bhailo and deusi songs in return for money and sweets, and Kathmandu's alleys are lit with lamps and electric strings. The fourth day includes Govardhan Puja and, for the Newar community, Mha Puja, a ritual of self-worship that also marks the Nepal Sambat new year with parades through Kathmandu. The last day, Bhai Tika, sees sisters give their brothers seven-coloured tika and garlands of makhamali flowers.

Tihar is an easy festival to enjoy as a visitor. The weather is usually clear and dry, Kathmandu and Patan look their best after dark on Laxmi Puja, and there are fewer closures than at Dashain. Indian visitors who celebrate Diwali at home often find the overlap with Tihar dates a reason to travel, so we suggest booking hotels early.
tips: Walk through Asan, Indra Chowk or Patan's lanes after 7 pm on Laxmi Puja for the best lamp displays.
Kukur Tihar is a good day for photographs of garlanded dogs; ask owners before photographing pets close up.
Tihar often overlaps Diwali, so Indian travellers should book hotels and flights two months ahead.

faqs.q: Is Tihar the same as Diwali?
faqs.a: Tihar and Diwali are closely related and fall in the same lunar period, with Laxmi Puja at the centre of both. Tihar is longer, five days, and has distinctly Nepali elements: worship of crows, dogs and cows, deusi-bhailo carol singing, the Newar Mha Puja and New Year, and Bhai Tika between brothers and sisters on the final day.

faqs.q: When is Tihar in 2026?
faqs.a: Tihar falls around the new moon of Kartik, usually late October or early November, roughly three weeks after Dashain. In 2026 Laxmi Puja is expected in early November. Exact dates are fixed by Nepal's calendar each year, so check current status before you travel. We confirm dates when we finalise your package.

faqs.q: What is Kukur Tihar?
faqs.a: Kukur Tihar is the second day of Tihar, dedicated to dogs. Families put a marigold garland and a red tika on their dogs and feed them meat, eggs or treats, and many people do the same for street dogs. Nepal Police dogs also receive a ceremony. It is one of the most photographed days of the festival.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see Tihar lights in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: The old trading lanes of Asan and Indra Chowk, the area around Kathmandu Durbar Square and Patan's Mangal Bazaar look best on Laxmi Puja night, with oil lamps on steps and windows. Bhaktapur is quieter but very atmospheric. Go after 7 pm, walk with a guide in the narrow lanes, and watch for firecrackers.

name: Indra Jatra
when: Aug–Sep, eight days in the lunar month of Yanla (Bhadra)
summary: Kathmandu's biggest street festival, eight days at the end of the monsoon centred on Kathmandu Durbar Square. A tall wooden pole is raised for the god Indra, masked Lakhey and Pulukisi dancers roam the streets and the living goddess Kumari is pulled through the old town in her chariot.
body: Indra Jatra marks the end of the monsoon and gives thanks to Indra, the Vedic god of rain. It opens with the raising of the yosin, a tall wooden pole brought from the forest and set upright in front of Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu Durbar Square. For the following days, images of Akash Bhairav are displayed across the old town, the great mask of Seto Bhairav at Hanuman Dhoka is uncovered, and at certain hours rice beer flows from a pipe in its mouth to a crowd hoping to catch a sip.

The festival's most watched moment is Kumari Jatra, when the Kumari, a young girl worshipped as a living goddess, leaves her house on Durbar Square and is drawn through the old city in a wooden chariot, followed by chariots of Ganesh and Bhairav. Masked dancers perform in the square in the evenings: the red-faced Lakhey demon, Pulukisi the elephant, and the Dasavatar dances of Vishnu's ten forms. The pole is lowered on the final day.

For visitors, Indra Jatra is a rare chance to see Newar Kathmandu at full volume, but it falls at the tail of the monsoon, so expect some rain and cloudy mountain views. Crowds in the square are dense on chariot days; we book a guide who knows where to stand and plan the rest of the trip for drier hills.
tips: Arrive at Kathmandu Durbar Square at least an hour before the Kumari chariot sets off to find a safe viewpoint.
Carry a light rain jacket, as late-monsoon showers are common in September.
Keep phones and wallets secure in the crowds around Hanuman Dhoka and Indra Chowk.

faqs.q: When is Indra Jatra held?
faqs.a: Indra Jatra runs for eight days in the Newar lunar month of Yanla, which usually falls in late August or September. The Kumari chariot procession takes place on set days within the festival. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. We can build a Kathmandu city break around the main chariot day.

faqs.q: Can tourists see the Kumari during Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: Yes. The Kumari Jatra chariot procession through Kathmandu's old town is the most public appearance of the living goddess each year. Thousands line the route from Basantapur through Indra Chowk and Asan. Photography of the procession from a distance is generally accepted, but do not use flash and follow any instructions from organisers or police.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting Nepal in September for Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: If culture is your priority, yes. Indra Jatra shows Kathmandu's Newar traditions at their most lively. The trade-off is weather: September is the end of the monsoon, so expect some rain, hazy mountains and occasional road delays. Pair it with valley sightseeing rather than mountain flights, which are more likely to be cancelled in cloud.

faqs.q: What happens at Seto Bhairav during Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: The large gilded mask of Seto Bhairav at Hanuman Dhoka, normally kept behind a lattice screen, is uncovered for the festival. At set times rice beer is poured so it flows from a pipe in the mouth, and people crowd forward to drink, believing it brings good fortune. Catching the small fish placed in the flow is thought especially lucky.

name: Bisket Jatra
when: April, nine days around Nepali New Year (mid-April)
summary: Bhaktapur's New Year festival in mid-April, when the chariot of the god Bhairav is hauled through the old town by rival halves of the city in a tug of war. A 25 m lingo pole is raised and toppled at Yoshin Khel to mark the start of the Nepali year.
body: Bisket Jatra, also written Biska Jatra, is Bhaktapur's great spring festival and lasts nine days around Nepali New Year in mid-April. It begins in Taumadhi Square beside the five-storey Nyatapola temple, where the heavy three-tiered chariot of Bhairav is assembled. Teams from the upper and lower halves of the town take hold of thick ropes on either side and pull against each other, and the side that drags the chariot into its own quarter is said to gain good fortune for the year. The tug of war can last hours and becomes loud and crowded.

On the eve of the New Year, at Yoshin Khel near the Khalna area, crowds raise a tall wooden pole, the lingo or yosin, hung with long cloth banners said to represent two serpents. The next evening it is pulled down, and the moment it falls marks the start of the new year. Over the following days neighbouring villages such as Thimi hold their own processions, with Sindoor Jatra in Thimi covering the streets in orange vermilion powder.

April is a good month to be in the valley: days are warm at 25 to 28 °C, rhododendrons bloom on the hills, and Bisket Jatra gives you a festival that is still run by the town for itself. Stay overnight in Bhaktapur if you can, because the chariot pulling continues after day-trippers leave.
tips: Watch the chariot tug of war from a raised café or temple step around Taumadhi, not in front of the wheels.
Stay a night in Bhaktapur during the festival, as evening events continue after day visitors go back to Kathmandu.
Bring clothes you do not mind staining if you plan to visit Thimi for Sindoor Jatra.

faqs.q: When is Bisket Jatra celebrated?
faqs.a: Bisket Jatra runs for nine days around Nepali New Year, which falls in mid-April, usually 13 or 14 April. The lingo pole is raised on the eve of the New Year and toppled the following evening. Exact dates follow Nepal's calendar, so check current status before you travel. Bhaktapur's hotels fill early for the festival week.

faqs.q: Is Bisket Jatra safe for tourists?
faqs.a: It is generally safe if you keep your distance from the chariot. The tug of war between the two halves of town can be rough, the chariot sometimes lurches or tips, and crowds surge around it. Watch from a raised step, rooftop café or temple plinth near Taumadhi Square, keep children close and follow your guide's advice.

faqs.q: Do I need a ticket to see Bisket Jatra?
faqs.a: There is no separate festival ticket, but foreign visitors entering Bhaktapur pay the town's heritage entry fee, around NPR 1,800 for foreigners and NPR 500 for SAARC nationals, including Indians. Keep the ticket with you, as it is checked at entry points; fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Bisket Jatra and Sindoor Jatra?
faqs.a: Bisket Jatra is Bhaktapur's main New Year festival with the Bhairav chariot and the lingo pole. Sindoor Jatra takes place in neighbouring Thimi on New Year's Day, when palanquins of local deities are carried around the town and people throw orange vermilion powder, leaving streets and crowds coloured. Many visitors see both on the same trip.

name: Maha Shivaratri at Pashupatinath
when: Feb–Mar, 14th night of the waning moon in Falgun
summary: The great night of Shiva, held in February or March, when hundreds of thousands of devotees and sadhus from Nepal and India gather at Pashupatinath. The temple stays open through the night, fires burn along the Bagmati and the whole precinct turns into a pilgrim camp.
body: Maha Shivaratri is the most important night of the year at Pashupatinath, Nepal's holiest Shiva temple. In the days before, sadhus arrive from across India and Nepal, some walking for weeks, and camp around the temple grounds and the forested Mrigasthali slope above the river, many with ash-covered bodies and sacred fires. Pilgrims queue from before dawn for darshan of the Shiva lingam, and the queues can stretch for well over a kilometre, moving slowly through the day.

Through the night devotees fast, sing bhajans and keep vigil. Lamps and dhuni fires burn along the ghats of the Bagmati, and the temple remains open far longer than usual. Children in Kathmandu traditionally stop passers-by with a rope across the lane to collect small coins for wood, and bonfires are lit in neighbourhoods to keep warm on what is usually a cold late-winter night. The Nepal Army holds a ceremonial event at Tundikhel in Kathmandu on the day.

For Hindu pilgrims from India, Shivaratri at Pashupatinath ranks among the major Shaiva pilgrimages, and we see many groups combine it with a valley temple circuit. Expect heavy security, road closures around Gaushala and Chabahil, and hotels near the temple full weeks ahead. Non-Hindus can watch from the eastern bank terraces but cannot enter the main courtyard.
tips: Join the darshan queue before 4 am or late at night for shorter waits, and carry water and a light snack if you are not fasting.
Book Kathmandu hotels at least six weeks ahead, and expect road closures around Gaushala and Chabahil.
Ask before photographing sadhus; many expect a small offering, and some decline photographs altogether.

faqs.q: When is Maha Shivaratri at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Maha Shivaratri falls on the 14th night of the waning moon in the month of Falgun, usually in February or early March. The main crowds arrive the evening before and stay through the night and following day. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel; we confirm them when we plan your yatra.

faqs.q: How long is the darshan queue on Shivaratri?
faqs.a: On the main day the queue for darshan at Pashupatinath can take four to eight hours, sometimes longer at peak times in the morning. Queues are usually shorter very early, before 4 am, or late at night. Senior citizens and people with disabilities sometimes have separate lines; check on arrival with temple volunteers and police.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit Pashupatinath on Shivaratri?
faqs.a: Non-Hindus cannot enter the main temple courtyard at any time, including on Shivaratri. They can buy the visitor ticket and watch from the terraces on the eastern bank of the Bagmati, walk among the sadhu camps and see the fires and crowds. Expect heavy security and restricted routes on the day, and follow police instructions.

faqs.q: Is it safe for senior pilgrims to attend Shivaratri at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Yes, with planning. Crowds are very large and queues long, so we suggest seniors go for darshan in the days just before or after the main night, or very early in the morning, with a guide and a vehicle waiting close by. Wear warm layers, as February nights in Kathmandu fall to around 3 to 5 °C.
